title: Find every bridge, even when edges repeat
description:
An edge of an undirected graph is a bridge when deleting that one edge leaves the graph in more separate pieces than it was in before.

Implement a function called Bridges that receives the number of vertices and a list of edges, and returns the positions in that list of every edge that is a bridge, in ascending order. Vertices are numbered from zero. Each edge is a pair of vertices, which can be written in either order, and an edge's position is its index in the list, starting from zero.

Bridges(5, [[1, 0], [0, 2], [2, 1], [0, 3], [3, 4]]) -> [3, 4]. That graph is a triangle on 0, 1, 2 with a tail 0 - 3 - 4. Deleting either tail edge cuts something off, but deleting any one side of the triangle still leaves its three vertices joined by the other two sides.

The same two vertices can be joined by more than one edge, and then no edge between them is a bridge, because deleting one copy leaves the others: Bridges(3, [[0, 1], [1, 2], [1, 2]]) -> [0]. This is why the answer is positions in the list and not vertex pairs. When the search walks back from a vertex, only the one edge it arrived along should be ignored, not every edge leading to the vertex it came from.

The hidden tests also check: a graph with no edges, and a ring, which both return an empty list; an edge from a vertex to itself, which is never a bridge; a graph in separate pieces, including a vertex with no edges, so every piece has to be examined and not just the one vertex 0 is in; and a list of edges ordered so the bridges are found in the reverse of their list order, which still has to come back ascending.

This card asks for the fastest solution, and the tests enforce it: one of them is a graph of a hundred thousand vertices with a two-second limit. Deleting one edge at a time and checking whether the graph is still connected gives the right answer but is far too slow. The whole graph has to be settled in a single traversal that visits each vertex and each edge once.
objective: Recall the linear-time bridge-finding algorithm: give each vertex a discovery time and a low value, lower the low value from a child's low value after visiting it and from a visited neighbor's discovery time otherwise, and mark the edge to a child as a bridge when the child's low value is strictly greater than the parent's discovery time. Skip only the edge you arrived along, identified by its position, so that a second copy of that edge still counts as a way back.
